title: Part 2, Chapter 30
paragraphs: Of Don Quixote's adventure with a beautiful huntress

Knight and squire returned to their animals dejected and in a thoroughly sour mood—Sancho especially, for anything that touched their store of money touched his very heart, and whenever any of it was taken from him he felt as though someone had plucked out the apples of his eyes. So, without a word passing between them, they mounted and rode away from the famous river, Don Quixote sunk in thoughts of his love, Sancho brooding over his hopes of advancement, which at that moment seemed to him very far from being realized. Fool though he was, he could see plainly enough that his master's actions were all, or nearly all, completely senseless, and he began looking for a chance to slip away from his service one day and go home, without offering any explanation or saying any goodbye. Fortune, however, arranged things in a manner very different from what he had in mind.

It happened that the next day, toward sunset, as he came out of a wood, Don Quixote looked across a green meadow and noticed some people at the far end of it; drawing nearer, he saw that it was a hawking party. Closer still, he made out among them a lady of graceful bearing, mounted on a snow-white palfrey or hackney fitted with green trappings and a silver-mounted side-saddle. The lady herself was dressed in green, so richly and magnificently that she seemed magnificence itself in human form. On her left hand she carried a hawk, which convinced Don Quixote that she must be some great lady and the mistress of the whole hunting party—as indeed she was. So he said to Sancho, “Run, Sancho, my son, and tell that lady on the palfrey with the hawk that I, the Knight of the Lions, kiss the hands of her exalted beauty, and that if her excellence grants me leave, I will come and kiss them in person and put myself at her service in whatever lies within my power and her highness may command. And watch how you speak, Sancho—take care not to wedge any of your proverbs into the message.”
“A fine one you've found to wedge any in!” said Sancho. “You can trust me with that! This isn't the first time in my life I've carried messages to high and exalted ladies.”
“Apart from the one you carried to the lady Dulcinea,” said Don Quixote, “I am not aware that you have carried any other, at least not in my service.”

“True enough,” replied Sancho; “but a good payer isn't troubled by his pledges, and in a house where there's plenty, supper is quickly on the table. What I mean is, there's no need to tell me anything or warn me about anything—I'm ready for whatever comes and know a little about everything.”
“I believe it, Sancho,” said Don Quixote. “Go then, and good luck to you, and God speed you on your way.”

Sancho set off at full tilt, driving Dapple beyond his usual pace, and reached the spot where the beautiful huntress was waiting. Dismounting, he knelt before her and said, “Fair lady, that knight you see over there, the Knight of the Lions by name, is my master, and I am a squire of his—at home they call me Sancho Panza. This same Knight of the Lions, who until recently went by the name of the Knight of the Rueful Countenance, sends me to ask whether it might please your highness to grant him leave so that, with your permission, approval, and consent, he may come and carry out his desire, which is—as he says and I believe—to serve your exalted loftiness and beauty. And if you grant it, your ladyship will be doing something that redounds to your honor, and he will receive a most distinguished favor and happiness.”

“Truly, squire,” said the lady, “you have delivered your message with every formality such messages demand. Stand up—it is not fitting that the squire of so great a knight as he of the Rueful Countenance, of whom we have heard a great deal in these parts, should stay on his knees. Rise, my friend, and tell your master that he is welcome to the service of myself and of the duke my husband, at a country house we keep nearby.”

Sancho stood up, as charmed by the good lady's beauty as by her well-bred manner and her courtesy, but most of all by her saying that she had heard of his master, the Knight of the Rueful Countenance; if she did not call him Knight of the Lions, it was doubtless only because he had taken that name so recently. “Tell me, brother squire,” asked the duchess (whose actual title is not known), “this master of yours—is he not the one about whom a history has been published, called ‘The Ingenious Gentleman, Don Quixote of La Mancha,’ who has as the lady of his heart a certain Dulcinea del Toboso?”

“The very same, señora,” replied Sancho; “and that squire of his who appears, or ought to appear, in the said history under the name of Sancho Panza, is me—unless they swapped me in the cradle, I mean in the printing press.”
“All of this delights me,” said the duchess. “Go, brother Panza, and tell your master that he is welcome on my estate, and that nothing could happen to me that would give me greater pleasure.”

Sancho went back to his master overjoyed with this gratifying answer, and reported everything the great lady had said, praising to the skies, in his rustic way, her rare beauty, her graceful liveliness, and her courtesy. Don Quixote sat up smartly in his saddle, planted himself firmly in his stirrups, adjusted his visor, spurred Rocinante, and rode forward with an easy air to kiss the duchess's hands. She, meanwhile, had sent for the duke her husband and, while Don Quixote was approaching, told him the whole story of the message. Since both of them had read the First Part of this history and knew from it about Don Quixote's mad streak, they awaited him with the keenest delight and eagerness to make his acquaintance, intending to play along with his fancy and agree with everything he said, and, for as long as he stayed with them, to treat him as a knight-errant, with all the ceremonies customary in the books of chivalry they had read—for they themselves were very fond of such books.

Don Quixote now rode up with his visor raised, and as he made to dismount, Sancho hurried over to hold his stirrup for him; but in climbing down from Dapple he had the bad luck to catch his foot in one of the ropes of the pack-saddle in such a way that he could not work it loose, and he was left dangling there with his face and chest on the ground. Don Quixote, who was not accustomed to dismounting without someone holding his stirrup, and assuming that Sancho had already arrived to hold it, swung himself off with a lurch and dragged Rocinante's saddle down after him—it must have been badly girthed—so that saddle and rider both ended up on the ground, to his considerable embarrassment and with plenty of curses muttered through his teeth against the unfortunate Sancho, whose foot was still caught in its shackle. The duke ordered his huntsmen to go to the aid of knight and squire, and they lifted up Don Quixote, badly shaken by his fall; limping, he advanced as best he could to kneel before the noble pair. This the duke would on no account allow; instead, dismounting from his own horse, he went and embraced Don Quixote, saying, “I am sorry, Sir Knight of the Rueful Countenance, that your first experience on my land should have been as unlucky a one as we have just witnessed; but the carelessness of squires is often the cause of worse accidents.”

“What has befallen me in meeting you, mighty prince,” replied Don Quixote, “cannot be called unfortunate, even if my fall had carried me all the way to the bottom of the bottomless pit, for the glory of having seen you would have raised me up and rescued me from it. My squire—God's curse upon him—is better at loosening his tongue to talk nonsense than at tightening a saddle's girths to keep it steady. But however I find myself, fallen or upright, on foot or on horseback, I shall always be at your service and at that of my lady the duchess, your worthy consort, worthy queen of beauty and supreme princess of courtesy.”
“Gently, Señor Don Quixote of La Mancha,” said the duke; “where my lady Doña Dulcinea del Toboso is concerned, it is not right that other beauties should be praised.”

Sancho, who by now had freed himself from his entanglement, was standing close by, and before his master could answer he said, “There's no denying it, and it must be insisted on, that my lady Dulcinea del Toboso is very beautiful; but the hare leaps up where you least expect it, and I've heard it said that what we call nature is like a potter who makes vessels out of clay, and whoever can make one fine vessel can just as easily make two, or three, or a hundred. I say this because, by my faith, my lady the duchess is in no way behind my mistress the lady Dulcinea del Toboso.”

Don Quixote turned to the duchess and said, “Your highness may be sure that no knight-errant in this world ever had a more talkative or more amusing squire than mine, and he will prove the truth of what I say if your highness is pleased to accept my services for a few days.”

To which the duchess answered, “That worthy Sancho is amusing I consider a very good thing, because it is a sign that he is shrewd; for wit and liveliness, Señor Don Quixote, as you well know, do not settle in dull minds, and since good Sancho is witty and lively, I hereby pronounce him shrewd.”
“And talkative,” Don Quixote added.
“All the better,” said the duke, “for many amusing things cannot be said in few words. But so as not to waste time talking, come, great Knight of the Rueful Countenance—”
“Of the Lions, your highness should say,” said Sancho, “for there's no Rueful Countenance, nor any such figure, anymore.”

“He of the Lions, then,” the duke went on. “I say, let Sir Knight of the Lions come to a castle of mine close by, where he will be given the reception owed to so exalted a person, the kind the duchess and I are accustomed to offer all knights-errant who come our way.”

By this time Sancho had set and girthed Rocinante's saddle, and once Don Quixote was on his back and the duke had mounted a fine horse, they placed the duchess between them and set out for the castle. The duchess asked Sancho to ride at her side, for she took endless pleasure in listening to his shrewd remarks. Sancho needed no urging; he worked himself in between her and the duke, who counted it rare good fortune to be receiving such a knight-errant and such a homespun squire at their castle.
